strengths: The paper addresses a timely and central topic in causal structure learning, providing a compelling counterweight to recent continuous-optimization approaches by showing that discrete order-based search can be both significantly faster and more accurate.

The algorithmic improvements are technically sound and well-engineered: warm-starting Grow-Shrink across neighboring orders, rank-1 dynamic Cholesky updates/downdates for BIC score evaluation, and a residual-variance-based order initialization that resolves failure modes on path graphs.

The empirical evaluation is extensive and thorough, covering diverse topologies (Erdős-Rényi, scale-free, paths, bnlearn benchmarks), multiple metrics (CPDAG SHD and AID), comparison against an exact dynamic programming baseline, and robustness checks (non-Gaussian noise, unstandardized data, Onion method).

The authors provide transparent and nuanced insights into the interplay between score optimization and finite-sample ground truth recovery (e.g., showing that on Pathfinder, optimizing BIC further via ILS yields better scores than the true graph despite higher SHD, highlighting identifiability limits under finite samples).
The paper is very well-written, clearly organized, and accompanied by an open-source Rust implementation with Python/R bindings.
weaknesses: The technical and theoretical novelty is somewhat evolutionary: the search framework builds directly on BOSS (Andrews et al., 2023), rank-one Cholesky updates are standard tools in numerical linear algebra, and ILS is a classic metaheuristic.

The method is inherently specialized to linear models evaluated under Gaussian BIC; extending the dynamic matrix update speedups to non-linear models or discrete Bayesian networks is non-trivial and not supported by the current formulation.

While the wall-clock comparisons against Tetrad implementations (Java, multithreaded) are favorable to FLOP (single-threaded Rust), presenting platform-independent metrics (e.g., number of score evaluations or parent candidates evaluated) would make the computational comparison even more conclusive.

strengths: Practical and timely contribution: The paper addresses a central debate in causal discovery (discrete search vs. continuous relaxation methods such as NOTEARS/DAGMA) by showing that discrete order-based search can be made orders of magnitude faster and highly accurate on linear ANMs.

Well-motivated algorithmic enhancements: The four proposed components—warm-starting grow-shrink from previous parent sets, dynamic Cholesky rank-one updates for Gaussian BIC scoring, regression-based order initialization (which resolves known failure modes on path graphs), and Iterated Local Search (ILS)—fit together cohesively and yield significant speed and accuracy gains.

Comprehensive empirical evaluation: The benchmarking is extensive and methodologically sound, evaluating CPDAG SHD, AID, and runtime across ER graphs, scale-free graphs, path graphs, and real-world bnlearn graphs, along with robustness checks against varsortability (unstandardized data, Onion method) and non-Gaussian noise.

Valuable empirical insights: The paper clearly illustrates that in many benchmark regimes, discrete BIC optimization is practically solved, and highlights the phenomenon where deeper search finds graphs with strictly higher likelihood/BIC than the true graph due to finite-sample limitations rather than search failure.
High-quality implementation: The authors provide a fast, single-threaded Rust implementation with Python and R bindings, making the tool readily useful for practitioners and researchers.
weaknesses: Limited to linear additive noise settings: The fast scoring via dynamic Cholesky updates and the regression-based initial ordering rely heavily on linearity (and Gaussian BIC), leaving non-linear or non-parametric settings beyond the scope of this work.

Incremental theoretical novelty: The theoretical results (Lemma 3.2 and Theorem 3.3) are relatively straightforward extensions of existing asymptotic correctness proofs for grow-shrink (Margaritis 2003; Lam et al., 2022). The primary contributions are algorithmic and engineering-driven rather than foundational theory.

Implementation-dependent runtime comparisons: In runtime comparisons against Tetrad (BOSS, PC, GES), the single-threaded Rust implementation is compared directly against multi-threaded Java code, which introduces language/runtime confounding into the wall-clock comparisons (although Figure 2 helpfully isolates the algorithmic ablation within FLOP itself).

strengths: Substantial computational speedup: By combining warm-started parent selection with O(k^2) rank-one Cholesky factor updates/downdates, the proposed FLOP algorithm achieves orders-of-magnitude speedups over existing order-based discrete search algorithms like BOSS, scaling cleanly up to 500 nodes.

Principled algorithmic additions: The residual-variance initialization strategy effectively targets a notable failure mode of order-based search on path graphs, while the Iterated Local Search (ILS) metaheuristic provides a practical anytime framework to trade computation for higher recovery accuracy.

Sound theoretical backing: Lemma 3.2 and Theorem 3.3 establish that the warm-started grow-shrink procedure preserves the restricted Markov boundary property and asymptotically recovers a Markovian DAG.

Thorough and insightful empirical evaluation: The benchmarking spans diverse graph topologies (Erdos-Renyi, scale-free, paths, bnlearn benchmarks), noise settings, and evaluation metrics (SHD, AID, BIC scores, and runtime). The analysis also provides valuable critical perspectives on continuous optimization baselines (DAGMA) and finite-sample score-optimality versus true graph identification.
weaknesses: Incremental conceptual novelty: The foundational search framework is adapted directly from BOSS (Andrews et al., 2023) and GRaSP (Lam et al., 2022). The core contributions—warm-starting grow-shrink, rank-one Cholesky updates, and ILS—represent smart engineering and adaptation of established numerical and metaheuristic techniques rather than fundamentally new structure learning paradigms.

Narrow model scope: The method and its key computational optimizations (especially the Cholesky updates and variance-based initialization) are tightly bound to linear Gaussian additive noise models (ANMs), limiting immediate applicability to nonlinear systems or categorical/discrete data.

Implementation and runtime attribution: While the single-threaded Rust implementation demonstrates impressive wall-clock speed, comparing it directly to multi-threaded Java (Tetrad) and Python implementations convolves language/runtime-level optimizations with pure algorithmic efficiency gains.

strengths: Compelling algorithmic contribution: The paper introduces FLOP, which synergistically combines warm-started grow-shrink, rank-1 dynamic Cholesky score updates, principled order initialization, and iterated local search (ILS). Each component is technically well-justified and directly addresses concrete computational or statistical bottlenecks in order-based DAG search.

Dramatic empirical speed and scaling advantages: FLOP achieves up to two orders of magnitude speedup over BOSS and scales effortlessly to graphs with 500 nodes where existing discrete methods time out, all while maintaining single-threaded execution.

Superior recovery accuracy and metaheuristic flexibility: By leveraging the saved compute into iterated local search (ILS), FLOP substantially improves finite-sample structural recovery (SHD and AID), matching exact exponential-time score-based solvers on dense graphs.

Thoughtful conceptual discussion on score optimization vs. score specification: The paper convincingly demonstrates that when discovery errors occur on finite samples, FLOP often finds DAGs with strictly lower (better) BIC than the ground truth. This neatly decouples the optimization challenge from the score identifiability/misspecification challenge, providing a valuable corrective to common assumptions in the causal discovery literature.
High reproducibility and practical utility: The method is accompanied by a clean, ready-to-use Rust implementation with Python bindings.
weaknesses: Scope currently focused on linear Gaussian ANMs: The rank-1 Cholesky update and local variance derivation rely on linear Gaussian models; adapting these computational speedups to non-linear models or non-parametric scores is non-trivial.

Algorithmic elements are largely adaptations of existing paradigms: While their assembly is elegant and effective, the core components (order search via reinsertion, rank-1 matrix update/downdate, ILS) are adaptations of well-established techniques from combinatorial optimization and numerical linear algebra rather than entirely novel algorithmic paradigms.

Evaluation on truly real-world data remains challenging: As demonstrated on the Sachs and causalAssembly datasets, model misspecification remains a significant hurdle in practice where optimizing BIC does not necessarily track the true causal graph, though the authors candidly acknowledge and analyze this limitation.

strengths: The paper presents a coherent, well-executed, and practically impactful contribution to score-based causal structure learning, demonstrating that carefully optimized discrete search significantly outperforms continuous optimization relaxations and existing order-based searches.

The algorithmic improvements over BOSS are elegant and technically sound: warm-starting grow-shrink from the previous parent set (supported by Lemma 3.2 and Theorem 3.3) and leveraging rank-1 Cholesky updates/downdates to reduce local scoring cost from O(k^3) to O(k^2).
The proposed initialization strategy based on greedy Cholesky-based residual variance addresses an underappreciated failure mode of order-based causal discovery on long directed paths.

Extensive empirical evaluation across diverse settings: Erdos-Renyi, scale-free, path graphs, benchmark Bayesian networks (Alarm, Mildew, Barley, Pathfinder), and real/semi-synthetic datasets (causalAssembly, Sachs), measuring both SHD and Ancestor Adjustment Identification Distance (AID).

Valuable conceptual insights on finite-sample causal discovery, demonstrating empirically that FLOP often finds graphs scoring better on BIC than the ground-truth DAG, clarifying that optimization failure is not the main bottleneck in standard linear benchmarks.
High reproducibility and practical value with a standalone Rust implementation wrapped for Python (`flopsearch`).
weaknesses: The individual algorithmic ingredients (grow-shrink warm-starts, rank-one Cholesky updates, iterated local search with random swap perturbations) are well-known techniques in discrete optimization and numerical linear algebra, meaning the conceptual novelty is somewhat incremental on top of BOSS (Andrews et al., 2023).
The speedup from dynamic Cholesky factor updates is tailored to the linear Gaussian BIC, leaving extensions to non-linear or non-Gaussian causal discovery outside the primary algorithmic framework.

While the authors transparently note that BOSS was evaluated via Java/Tetrad multithreaded code and FLOP in Rust single-threaded, language-level differences confound the exact software speedup factor, although the internal ablations (pre-FLOP variants in Figure 2) successfully demonstrate the algorithmic speedups.

strengths: Substantial computational speedups over existing order-based methods: Combining warm-started Grow-Shrink with incremental rank-1 Cholesky updates reduces per-evaluation complexity and results in an over 100x speedup compared to BOSS, allowing discrete search to scale to 500 nodes in reasonable time.

Important conceptual takeaways for the causal structure learning community: The paper empirically demonstrates that discrete search frequently achieves equal or better BIC scores than the true DAG, disentangling optimization failure from finite-sample score misspecification and questioning the common narrative regarding the necessity of continuous relaxations.

Principled initialization and metaheuristic search: The correlation-based order initialization effectively resolves the longstanding failure mode of order search on long chain/path graphs, while the Iterated Local Search (ILS) framework turns available compute time into a directly actionable lever for solution quality.

Extensive and rigorous empirical evaluation: The benchmarking spans diverse graph topologies (ER, SF, chains), sample sizes, score differences, downstream causal metrics (AID as well as SHD), benchmark networks (Alarm, Barley, Mildew, Pathfinder), and semi-synthetic/real datasets (CausalAssembly, Sachs), accompanied by thorough ablations.
High reproducibility and practical utility: The method is provided as a fast, single-threaded Rust library with ready-to-use Python bindings.
weaknesses: Limited fundamental methodological novelty: The search strategy is primarily an engineering and algorithmic optimization of BOSS (Andrews et al., 2023) coupled with standard discrete optimization metaheuristics (Iterated Local Search) and textbook linear algebra (Cholesky rank-one updates).

Restricted scope of core speedups: The O(k^2) dynamic Cholesky scoring relies strictly on linear Gaussian models where scores derive from covariance submatrices; extending these fast updates to general non-linear or non-parametric scores is non-trivial.

Modest theoretical contributions: The theoretical results (Lemma 3.2 and Theorem 3.3) are direct adaptations of known Markov boundary recovery proofs (Margaritis, 2003; Lam et al., 2022) to the warm-started setting rather than major new theoretical insights.
